top.line: Palmer's four newsroom outputs, checked against a running newsroom
top.para: Jonathan Palmer asked on 10 October what a news business would look like with no human readers, naming four outputs beyond the article. Each is checked against newsroom.sgit.ai: graphs, version history, hashed op-eds and agent surfaces run, while selling the graph, propagating corrections and paying fact creators are only designed. Unlike Palmer, the newsroom publishes its data openly.

short.line: Structure, provenance and distribution run; the commerce does not
short.para: Structured intelligence runs, with a graph for all 74 articles and 160 nodes and 427 edges for World News Day. Continuous intelligence half runs: versions yes, propagating corrections no. Provenance runs through a hashed, openly readable vault, but nothing is paid. Distribution runs via llms.txt and markdown twins. The difference: publish the graph, sell fitted projections.

scenario.line: Modelling no human readers: synthetic users and agent costs
scenario.para: Palmer is right that most strategies assume the reader relationship will endure. The newsroom modelled the scenario twice: five synthetic users took 62 steps, raised 51 unanswered questions and 31 findings, and four of five left. An agent answering from five articles' graphs used a median of 2,579 tokens against 25,698 from the prose.

structured.line: Every article has a graph, and others' work too
structured.para: All 74 articles have a JSON graph of ideas, claims, methods and examples, rendered alongside the pages. For World News Day, 21 op-eds were frozen and turned into a graph of 160 nodes and 427 edges with downloadable files, and five agents catalogued 662 items across five articles. None of it is sold.

continuous.line: Versions are tracked from git; propagating corrections are not
continuous.para: Every article has a version history read from git at each build, with diff pages showing old and new text and ten amber edges marking older articles updated to point at newer ones. Carrying a correction to pages that cited the corrected claim is designed, not built, and there is no published way to report an error.

provenance.line: Provenance is explicit and checkable, but not yet commercial
provenance.para: The 21 op-eds were fetched once, frozen, hashed with SHA-256 and re-derived by a second program, with the vault's read key printed so anyone can check. Six roles have written behaviour policies. Commercial access is only designed: a 60, 25, 10, 5 revenue split and trust as a service, with nothing yet paid.

embedded.line: Agents get llms.txt, markdown twins, feeds and graphs
embedded.para: An llms.txt states what runs, every page has a markdown twin, and feeds and graphs are fetchable without rendering. Reading lists and personas travel in links. The value is measured: 25,698 tokens to read five articles against a median of 2,579 from their graphs. Agent packs, accounts and deltas remain proposals.

pay.line: Agents pay because served meaning costs less than reading
pay.para: The agent pays not to pay: a fitted projection and dated, signed claims save it more than they cost. Unlike Palmer's proprietary assets, the graphs are free and the vault key published, because provenance only the publisher can check is a promise. Human readers pay pence per page from a browser balance, with five-pound card top-ups.

article.line: The article stays, but stops organising the newsroom
article.para: The story is a graph and the article one projection, alongside summaries, decks, maps and briefings, though the prose is still written first because writing finds the argument. Palmer's closing line asks for a redesign of the data capture operating model; licensing archives sells the past once, while capturing structure continuously sells the present.

cultural.line: The technical change is cheap; the cultural one unproven
cultural.para: One person and a desk of agents produced 74 articles with graphs, versions, a hashed corpus, a vault and agent surfaces in eight weeks on static files. The cultural change cannot be demonstrated because this newsroom started with the graph. Local journalism may gain most, and one desk running the scenario in public is a cheap start.

limits.line: Nothing is sold, and one newsroom proves little
limits.para: The graphs are free and the only money moving is an optional five-pound top-up. Seventy-four articles by one author are a model, not evidence for a legacy newsroom. Selling the graph, paying fact creators, propagating corrections and agent packs are designed, not running. Palmer's lines are quoted verbatim; publishers can contact agent@riskmandate.ai.

sources.line: Sources: Palmer's post, the voice memo and screenshots
sources.para: Written by the site's agent from a voice memo of 11 October 2026, with quotations verbatim from Jonathan Palmer's LinkedIn post of 10 October. Screenshots show newsroom.sgit.ai at v0.8.0. Figures come from The agent is the reader, How to run synthetic users and One article, five readers, with related articles linked.
